name: Charter of the United Nations, Articles 2 and 51
claim: Sovereign equality, peaceful dispute resolution, prohibition of force and self-defence provide foundational legal constraints.
implication: No forced territorial recognition or coercive settlement proposal.

name: OHCHR civilian-protection report: September 2026
claim: At least 328 civilians killed and 2,105 injured in Ukraine during September 2026 (documented minimum).
implication: Prioritize verified civilian protection and warn against undercounting.

name: Reuters: IAEA-facilitated Zaporizhzhia repair truce
confidence: Medium–high; independent repair outcome not established here
claim: Rosatom reported a locally scoped IAEA-mediated truce for power-supply repairs.
implication: Test narrow technical pause models, not a claim of general ceasefire.

name: OSCE support for monitoring a negotiated settlement
claim: OSCE leadership indicated readiness to support implementation monitoring, if authorized.
implication: Explore consent-based monitoring mandates and funding.

name: ICRC: value of neutrality for humanitarian work
claim: Neutral, independent and impartial intermediary activities include repatriation and reconnecting families.
implication: Respect confidentiality; do not publish sensitive cases or impose advocacy roles.

name: World Bank Group support to Ukraine: March 2026
confidence: High for published estimate; projections uncertain
claim: February 2026 RDNA5 estimated nearly US$588 billion in reconstruction needs over the following decade.
implication: Financing designs need audits, prioritization and local ownership.

name: Trystero: official getting started and connection requirements
claim: Both peers must share app ID, room ID, signaling strategy and password; some network pairs need TURN.
implication: Opt-in peer connection with room-code diagnostics and honest TURN fallback.

name: Trystero: signaling strategies
claim: Default Trystero uses public Nostr relays; signaling and data transport are distinct.
implication: Never claim network or relay availability in offline mode.

name: UN General Assembly leadership on sovereignty and ceasefire
claim: UN General Assembly leadership reiterated Ukrainian sovereignty and internationally recognized borders, cessation of hostilities, and the importance of a UN Charter-based negotiated peace.
implication: Settlement proposals must disclose and test compatibility with international law; do not treat territorial coercion as consent.

name: Paris declaration on security guarantees
claim: Ukraine, the US and Coalition of the Willing participants stressed sovereign security and politically/legally binding guarantees to take effect after a ceasefire; pledges remain subject to their legal arrangements.
implication: Security arrangements require named guarantors, domestic authority, clear trigger, verification, and credible breach response.

name: E3 and Ukrainian leaders on negotiation conditions
claim: Leaders called for immediate ceasefire, negotiations beginning from the line of contact without changing borders by force, legally binding security guarantees, and appropriate EU/NATO consent for arrangements involving them.
implication: Distinguish negotiating starting points from territorial recognition; EU and NATO are not bound by external proposals without authorization.

name: OSCE Special Monitoring Mission to Ukraine — closed
claim: The OSCE Special Monitoring Mission to Ukraine ceased operations on 31 March 2022; it is not a presently deployed verification body.
implication: Any new mission needs its own authorization, mandate, security access, budget and compliance design.

name: OSCE: A Peaceful Presence, first five years of SMM
claim: Monitoring missions face mandate, access, safety and technical limitations; implementation mechanisms cannot be assumed from a signature alone.
implication: Specify monitor mandate, access, reporting, incident review, and obstruction outcomes separately.

name: ICRC neutral intermediary — role and consent
claim: ICRC may facilitate family links and exchanges as a neutral intermediary but can only act with agreement of the involved parties.
implication: Never nominate or represent ICRC without its own acceptance and the relevant parties’ agreement.

name: Reuters: Kremlin rejected proposed 60-day ceasefire
claim: Kremlin rejected a proposed short-term 60-day ceasefire tied to Ukrainian elections and emphasized seeking an overall long-term arrangement; not proof about acceptance of other proposals.
implication: Political willingness and acceptable sequencing cannot be deduced from interest in talks.

name: Reuters: Ukraine awaits details of proposed energy ceasefire
claim: Ukrainian president welcomed a proposed energy ceasefire in principle but said details and actual Russian compliance were needed amid continuing attacks.
implication: Announced proposals are not mutually signed or verified restraint agreements.

name: Reuters: Russian non-negotiable security-zone claim
claim: Putin publicly characterized a security zone in Ukrainian border regions as non-negotiable; this is a reported Russian position, not an internationally accepted legal arrangement.
implication: Record incompatibilities and test whether a draft is actually negotiable; do not convert asserted control into legal recognition.

name: Reuters: Kremlin supports Vatican aid initiative for Oleshky
claim: Kremlin said Russia would cooperate with a Vatican-backed humanitarian-aid proposal for Oleshky; this alone is not a verified, agreed and implemented ceasefire.
implication: Potential narrow humanitarian entry point still requires the other parties, independent access and safety guarantees.
